cues.zh: 而B-24轰炸机，这些轰炸机在一万五千到两万五千英尺之间飞行。这些飞机没有增压舱。飞行员和机组成员每次任务都要吸氧六到八个小时。稍后你们会看到一些相关照片。目标是摧毁交通基础设施、石油和燃油基础设施、飞机工业基础设施，以及其他任何为德国战争经济服务的东西。

cues.en: As soon as they took off from Britain, they were facing the German air defense system. And here's the stuff no movie maker ever knew. The Germans, in 1940, set up the Camugele Line. It was an integrated electronic air defense network that stretched from northern France all the way into Germany. Its job was to defend Germany from British and US bomber raids to warn and detect German air defense.
cues.zh: 他们刚从英国起飞，就面对着德国的防空系统。而这是电影制作人从来不知道的东西。德国人在1940年建立了Camugele防线。那是一个集成的电子防空网络，从法国北部一直延伸到德国境内。它的任务是保卫德国免受英美轰炸机空袭，为德国防空进行预警和探测。

cues.en: to target and aim their weapons and then destroy the bombers before they got to the targets. The Germans could see the British and American planes forming up 200 miles away. How'd they see the target? Here's the other piece you never saw in any war movie about World War II. They show the bombardier using an optical bomb sight. Works great when it's clear. It's optical. How do you bomb through a cloud? Great weather.
cues.zh: 好，他们正要开始轰炸，有人提到了云层问题。秋冬季节的欧洲上空，每月只有四天是晴天。照片拍得不错，显示天气很好。可他们怎么看到目标呢？这就是二战题材战争片里从没展示过的另一面。电影里演的是投弹手用光学瞄准具，晴天时确实好用，毕竟那是光学的。可怎么穿过云层轰炸呢？天气真好。

cues.en: By the way, that's flak dropping their bombs on a target. By the way, only about 30% of bombs even at the end of the war within a half a mile of the target. Precision bombing was an oxymoron. So what they finally decided to do and invented and installed by 1943 was air to ground radar. By the end of the war, every US and British bomber had a
cues.zh: 顺便说一句，那是高射炮在向目标投弹。顺便说一句，即便到了战争末期，也只有大约30%的炸弹落在目标半英里范围内。所谓“精确轰炸”本身就是个矛盾的说法。所以他们最终决定采用、并在1943年前安装到位的是空对地雷达。到战争结束时，每一架美国和英国的轰炸机都配备了

cues.en: bombing radar set. It meant for the first time they no longer needed to cancel missions when it was overcast over the target. These were pretty primitive, and all they did was paint an outline of kind of the major ground features. But it was good enough to develop map overlays to say, well, if you see a feature that looks like that, it's probably Hamburg. And so targets could be under Berlin, or maybe it's hopefully not London. Targets could be seen under the cloud in the rain.
cues.zh: 轰炸雷达。这意味着他们第一次不再需要因为目标上空阴天而取消任务。这些雷达相当原始，只能勾勒出主要地面特征的大致轮廓。但已经足够用来制作地图叠加图，据此判断：如果你看到某个特征长这样，那大概就是汉堡。于是目标可以在柏林上空被发现，或者但愿不是伦敦。目标可以在云层和雨中就被识别出来。

cues.en: The British installed this in mid-1943. The Americans took it and improved it a bit and put it in mass production on every British and American bomber. This will come back in another story a little later on. Now supposedly, this story and this talk is about the secret history of Silicon Valley. Well, this might be amusing or interesting. What the heck does World War II have to do with Silicon Valley? So let me just remind you about what's going on here.
cues.zh: 英国人在1943年中期把它投入使用。美国人拿去稍加改进，然后大规模生产，装到了每一架英国和美国的轰炸机上。这个话题稍后还会在另一个故事里再次出现。按理说，这个故事和这场演讲讲的是硅谷的秘密历史。好吧，这可能有点意思。但二战到底和硅谷有什么关系呢？让我先提醒你一下当时发生了什么。

cues.en: Horrific casualties. Google math challenge. For every 100 bombers on a mission, each mission, 4 to 20% wouldn't return. Holy cow, they're your age. And you had to fly 25 missions to go home, sobering. It was a priority to defeat German air defense system. Air defense system at its core was electronic. So story two.
cues.zh: 伤亡惨重。我们来算一笔数学账。每次任务中，每100架轰炸机，会有4%到20%无法返航。天哪，他们和你们年纪相仿。而且要飞满25次任务才能回家，真令人心寒。击败德国防空系统是头等大事。而防空系统的核心是电子技术。所以，第二个故事来了。

cues.en: was the development of an electronic shield in the middle of World War II called electronic warfare. And it was run by the most secret lab you probably never heard of called the Harvard Radio Research Lab, which was in Harvard. But it was a code name for the US countermeasures. And its goal was to reduce losses to fighters and flak. And it did it with a couple ways. First, the Germans didn't publish any papers on their radar.
cues.zh: 讲的是二战中期一种电子盾牌的研发，也就是电子战。它由一个你大概从没听说过的绝密实验室负责——哈佛无线电研究实验室，位于哈佛。它其实是美国电子对抗项目的代号。目标是降低战斗机和高射炮造成的损失。实现方式有几种。首先，德国人从不发表任何关于雷达的论文。

cues.en: There's no open source literature. Google wasn't around. So the first one was we needed to gather electronic intelligence and signals intelligence about the characteristics of these signals. Then we needed to develop devices to jam and confuse those radars. This was a top secret 800 person lab. The first thing to find and understand German air defense, we took a couple bombers and stripped all the bombs and racks and everything you can imagine out of them.
cues.zh: 没有任何公开文献，Google 也还没诞生。所以第一步，我们需要收集电子情报和信号情报，搞清这些信号的特征。然后我们需要开发干扰和迷惑这些雷达的设备。这是一个800人的绝密实验室。为了找到并摸清德国防空体系，我们拿了几架轰炸机，拆掉了所有炸弹、挂架和一切你能想到的东西。

cues.en: and packed them full of radar receivers, developed special purpose receivers that could go from 50 megahertz to 3 gigahertz. This is 1942. And flew these planes unarmed, over Germany, and recorded radar signals. Try to figure out frequency, power, pulse rate, et cetera. Once we understood that, we came up with some defenses. And the first one, believe it or not,
cues.zh: 把它们装满雷达接收器，研制出专用接收器，频率能从50兆赫覆盖到3吉赫兹。这可是1942年。然后让这些飞机不带武器飞越德国上空，记录雷达信号。试图弄清频率、功率、脉冲率等等。一旦搞明白了这些，我们就想出了对策。而第一个对策，信不信由你，

cues.en: was mechanical, not electronic. It turns out, if you cut pieces of reflective material, and I don't mean optically reflective, I mean radar reflective, to half the frequency of that radar, it would get false returns. You could jam the radar by throwing tinfoil out the back of a plane. The British called it window, we called it shaft. We used this to disrupt the German air defense.
cues.zh: 是机械的，不是电子的。原来，如果你把反光材料切成片——我不是说光学反光，是雷达反光——切到该雷达频率的一半，就会产生假回波。你可以从飞机尾部扔锡箔来干扰雷达。英国人管这叫window，我们叫shaft。我们用它来扰乱德国防空，

cues.en: by jamming the Würzburg frequencies for both ground control intercept and radar guided and our aircraft. It was first used over a city called Hamburg. And the first time this happened, we completely shut down the entire German air defense system. And it happened to be timed with a thousand bomber raid, which used incinerators for the first time to try to destroy a complete German city. Some of you might know the results over Hamburg.
cues.zh: 干扰维尔茨堡频率，既针对地面引导拦截，也针对雷达制导和我们自己的飞机。它首次用在汉堡这座城市上空。第一次使用时，我们彻底瘫痪了整个德国防空系统。而且恰好赶上千机轰炸，那次首次使用焚化炉，试图摧毁一整座德国城市。你们有些人可能知道汉堡的结果。

cues.en: In this first attempt, the crews literally opened the door and manually tossed out packets of CHAF. Automatic dispensers became later. This was so important. During the war, it used three quarters of all aluminum foil in the United States. Disappeared. No one understood why we were having an aluminum drive for CHAF. But then this Harvard Radio Research Lab started earning their money.
cues.zh: 在这第一次尝试中，机组人员简直是打开舱门，手动把一包包的干扰箔条扔出去。自动投放器是后来才有的。这太重要了。战争期间，它用掉了美国全部铝箔的四分之三。铝箔消失了。没人明白为什么我们要为干扰箔条搞铝材运动。但接着，这个哈佛无线电研究实验室开始证明自己的价值了。

cues.en: They systematically said, we're going to shut down every electronic component of German air defense. We're going to start by jamming those early warning radars. And we're going to put jammers on airplanes and blind the washermans, mammoths, and freers. And they built jammers to do that first on escort fighters that flew along with the bombers. And then, when there were enough of these devices, it went on every bomber.
cues.zh: 他们系统性地提出：我们要瘫痪德国防空系统的每一个电子部件。先从干扰那些预警雷达开始。还要把干扰机装上飞机，让 Wassermann、Mammut 和 Freya 致盲。他们造出干扰机，先装在随轰炸机飞行的护航战斗机上。等设备数量够了，就装到每架轰炸机上。

cues.en: Next thing was, let's jam the German anti-aircraft radar, the Würzburgs. We're going to shut down the flak. We built 24,000 of these jammers, put them on all the bombers. And then for the British at night, we need to jam the airborne radar on the fighters. And they built a set of devices to do that. Not only jam the fighter radar, but to jam the communications link between that fighter and its controller, trying to vector them in.
cues.zh: 下一步是：干扰德国的防空雷达，也就是 Würzburg。我们要压制高射炮。我们造了 24,000 台这种干扰机，装到所有轰炸机上。然后针对英国人的夜间行动，我们需要干扰战斗机上的机载雷达。他们造了一组设备来做这件事。不仅干扰战斗机雷达，还干扰战斗机和控制员之间的通信链路，让控制员无法引导它们拦截。

cues.en: Now, this was great. It was on all British bombers. By the end of the war in 1944 and 1945, a bomber stream had an integrated electronic defensive system that flew along with it. It had chaff. It had electronic intelligence planes, making sure there were no new German signals coming up or other radars. We were jamming the ground control intercept signals. And we were jamming against the AAA. And all this was integrated not only in the planes itself,
cues.zh: 这很厉害。它装到了所有英国轰炸机上。到 1944、1945 年战争结束时，一个轰炸机编队拥有随行的综合电子防御系统。它有箔条。它有电子情报飞机，确保没有新的德国信号或其他雷达出现。我们在干扰地面控制拦截信号。我们也在干扰高射炮。而这一切不仅集成在飞机本身，

cues.en: But by this time, there were dedicated planes that had nothing, nothing, no bombs, but racks full of jammers flying along with every bomber mission. Now, this is pretty important. An integral part of the World War II war effort, you never heard about it. So who ran the secret lab and became the father of electronic warfare? And what the heck does this still have to do with Silicon Valley? Because the Harvard Radio Research Lab
cues.zh: 但到这时，已经有专用飞机：什么都没有，没有炸弹，只有装满干扰机的挂架，随每次轰炸任务飞行。这很重要。它是二战作战中不可或缺的一部分，你却从没听说过。那么，谁掌管了那个秘密实验室，并成为电子战之父？而这到底跟硅谷还有什么关系？因为 Harvard Radio Research Lab

cues.en: which was the spin out of the MIT radiation lab, had 800 people. It wasn't like five guys that never heard of it. 800 people. The guy who ran it was Fred Terman of Stanford. Any of you from Stanford? Anybody ever see this Terman engineering building? It's where my office is.
cues.zh: 它是从 MIT 辐射实验室分拆出来的，有 800 人。不是什么只有五个从没听说过这回事的人。800 人。掌管它的是 Stanford 的 Fred Terman。你们有谁来自 Stanford 吗？有人见过这栋 Terman Engineering Building 吗？我的办公室就在那里。

cues.en: Fred Terman, if you do know about him, is known as the father of Silicon Valley, but not because he was the father of electronic warfare. He was known as the kindly professor who encouraged his students, Bill Hewlett and David Packard, to start a company. That's what Fred Terman is known for in Valley lore. And for those of us in the black world, we kind of laugh, because that's not who Fred Terman really was. Fred Terman was the father of the military industrial complex in Silicon Valley.
cues.zh: 如果你听说过 Fred Terman，他被称为硅谷之父，但并不是因为他是电子战之父。在大家的印象里，他是那位鼓励自己的学生 Bill Hewlett 和 David Packard 去创业的和蔼教授。在硅谷的传闻中，Fred Terman 就是因此闻名的。但对于我们这些接触机密军工圈的人来说，我们只会相视一笑，因为那根本不是真正的 Fred Terman。Fred Terman 实际上是硅谷军工复合体之父。

cues.en: He was dean of engineering in 1946, and he was provost in 1955. I want to talk about what happened in the Valley when Fred Terman came back from World War II, knowing what he knew and knowing what he did. Just for some history, in World War II, the Office of Scientific Research and Development enlisted university research in helping win the war.
cues.zh: 他在 1946 年担任工学院院长，1955 年出任教务长。我想聊聊 Fred Terman 带着他的见识和阅历从二战归来后，硅谷到底发生了什么。先补充一点历史背景，二战期间，科学研究与开发办公室（Office of Scientific Research and Development）动员高校科研力量来协助赢得战争。

cues.en: It was the first time the military said, no, no, no, we're not going to use our own labs to do advanced R&D, though we will. We're going to enlist all society, including university labs. And we're going to give out serious bucks for the first time to do this. $450 million was spent on weapons R&D. Good chunk of it with universities. MIT got $117 million. Caltech 83. Harvard and Columbia, 30. Dramatically changed.
cues.zh: 这是军方第一次表示，不不不，我们不能光用自己的实验室搞前沿研发——虽然我们也会做。我们要发动全社会的力量，包括高校实验室。而且我们破天荒地为此砸下了巨款。武器研发总共投入了 4.5 亿美元，其中很大一部分流向了大学。MIT 拿到了 1.17 亿美元，Caltech 拿了 8300 万，Harvard 和 Columbia 拿了 3000 万。这彻底改变了……

cues.en: the direction and velocity of those universities. Oh, and by the way, Stanford got 50 grand. 50 grand. Terman was so pissed he packed up and his old PhD advisor, Vannevar Bush, recruited him to head up the Harvard Radio Research Lab. Terman says, when he returns, this will never happen to Stanford again. His post-war strategy is to make Stanford a center of excellence for microwaves and electronics.
cues.zh: 那些大学的发展方向和前进速度。哦，顺便说一句，Stanford 只拿到了 5 万美元。才 5 万块。Terman 气得收拾铺盖走人，他的博士导师 Vannevar Bush 招揽他去主管 Harvard Radio Research Lab。Terman 说，等他回来，这种事绝不能再在 Stanford 重演。他的战后策略，就是要把 Stanford 打造成微波与电子领域的顶尖科研中心。

cues.en: cleistrons, traveling wave tubes, et cetera. And he's going to build Stanford with the MIT, not Harvard, model of military university collaboration from day one. Not going to be left out of the gravy train again. So Terman, being smart, said, hey, I had the world's best people in high power microwaves, radar, advanced electronics, paid for by the military sitting at Harvard. How can I get them at Stanford?
cues.zh: 速调管、行波管等等。他要从一开始，就按照 MIT 而不是 Harvard 的模式，把 Stanford 建成军方与大学合作的机构。这次他不想再错过利益列车。所以 Terman 很聪明，他想：我手头有世界上最优秀的高功率微波、雷达和先进电子学人才，他们拿着军方的经费，坐镇 Harvard。我怎样才能把他们弄到 Stanford 来？

cues.en: 11 of them now become faculty members. Pretty cute idea. He reassembles essentially the radio research lab, Cream of the Crop, at Stanford as faculty. And he sets up the electronic research laboratory, ERL, as part of the engineering department. And for the first four years, works on basic and unclassified research. Very benign, great idea. And got the first Office of Naval Research contract in 1946. ONR was the only
cues.zh: 其中 11 人后来成了 Stanford 的教员。这个主意相当妙。他基本上把无线电研究实验室的精英团队重新组建起来，作为教员带到 Stanford。他还在工程系下设立了电子研究实验室，也就是 ERL。前四年专注于基础研究和非机密研究。非常温和，是个好主意。1946 年，他还拿到了海军研究办公室的第一份合同。ONR 是军方中唯一

cues.en: part of the military, even interested in continuing military R&D. By 1950, Terman turns Stanford's electronics department into the MIT of the West. Well-known, really impressive. But the Korean War came. I don't know if any of you read history, but the Soviet Union was our ally in World War II. And after the war ended, things went bad pretty quickly. We thought we had a nuclear monopoly.
cues.zh: 有兴趣继续开展军事研发的部门。到 1950 年，Terman 把 Stanford 的电子系变成了西部的 MIT。名气很大，实力也非常强。但朝鲜战争爆发了。我不知道你们有没有读过历史，但苏联在第二次世界大战中曾是我们的盟友。战争结束后，局势很快恶化。我们原以为自己拥有核垄断。

cues.en: The Soviet Union detonated its first atomic weapon in 1949. They took over Eastern Europe, and the iron curtain came down pretty fast. And from what became our ally, very quickly became a, not only threat, but a nuclear-armed threat. It looked like communism was the winning bet. And then in 1951, North Korea invaded South Korea, and we joined yet again another war.
cues.zh: 苏联在 1949 年引爆了第一枚原子弹。他们控制了东欧，铁幕也很快降下。从曾经的盟友，苏联很快变成了不仅是威胁，而且是拥有核武器的威胁。看起来，共产主义才是赢家。然后在 1951 年，朝鲜入侵韩国，我们又一次参战。

cues.en: We saw communist conspiracy everywhere, and the Korean War truly changed the game, not only for the country's thinking, but for Terman's thinking as well. Spook work comes to Stanford. Terman sets up a classified department at Stanford, the Applied Electronics Lab.
cues.zh: 我们到处都看到了共产主义阴谋，朝鲜战争确实改变了局势，不仅改变了这个国家的思维，也改变了 Terman 的想法。秘密情报工作进入 Stanford。Terman 在 Stanford 建立了一个涉密部门，也就是应用电子实验室。

cues.en: and doubles the size of the electronics program, says, no, no, this will be separate from the unclassified work, but it made for the first time the University a full partner in this military industrial complex. We were doing serious weapons research at Stanford. Everything we knew in World War II, we're doing, but we're doing it more. Just to give you a context, this was paranoia time and probably not unrealistically.
cues.zh: 并将电子学项目的规模扩大了一倍。他说，不，这和非涉密工作必须分开，但这第一次让大学成为这个军工复合体的全面合作伙伴。我们在 Stanford 开展着严肃的武器研究。二战期间我们掌握的一切都在做，只是做得更多。给大家一个背景，当时是偏执盛行的年代，而且这种偏执可能并非毫无根据。

cues.en: The Cold War battlefield moved from Germany to 500 miles to the east. Somebody's probably pointing out their hometown next to the ICBM site. There was a real fear this time of a nuclear Pearl Harbor, because the Soviet Union was a closed country. Electronic countermeasures, electronic intelligence, signal intelligence, all become critical, and that's what Stanford's expertise was known for, for its customers.
cues.zh: 冷战的战场从德国向东移动了 500 英里。可能有人正指着洲际弹道导弹基地旁边的家乡。这一次，人们真的担心会遭遇一场核珍珠港事件，因为苏联是一个封闭的国家。电子对抗、电子情报、信号情报，全都变得至关重要，而这正是 Stanford 为其客户所熟知的专长。

cues.en: the National Security Agency, the Central Intelligence Agency, and the arms of the military. This Cold War is an electronic war. This Russian air defense system that they set up is Germany times 10, because not only are there fighters and anti-aircraft guns, but they start building surface-to-air missiles. They start adding sophisticated radar to not only their night fighters, but their day fighters. So the big job was, how do you understand
cues.zh: 这些客户包括国家安全局、中央情报局以及军方机构。冷战是一场电子战争。他们在德国部署的这套俄罗斯防空系统，规模是原来的十倍，因为那里不仅有战斗机和高射炮，他们还开始建造地对空导弹。他们开始给夜间战斗机和日间战斗机都配备复杂的雷达。所以当时最大的任务就是：如何了解

cues.en: the radar order of battle in the Soviet Union. And now, they don't have V2s, they're starting to build intercontinental ballistic missiles. How can we monitor the telemetry that they put on all their test missiles and figure out its performance? How do we do photo reconnaissance to find out where the missile silos are? And how do we monitor their growing navy? And even more so, how do we even identify where their production facilities are and production capabilities?
cues.zh: 苏联的雷达作战部署。那时他们已经不再只有 V-2 火箭，而是开始建造洲际弹道导弹。我们如何监测他们安装在所有试验导弹上的遥测设备，并判断导弹的性能？我们如何进行航空摄影侦察，找出导弹发射井的位置？我们又如何监视他们不断扩张的海军？更进一步，我们甚至要如何确认他们的生产设施在哪里，以及他们的生产能力？

cues.en: for their nuclear weapons. All this required not only photo evidence, but required electronic and signals intelligence. So Stanford throws its hat in, joins the black world. Terman decides to take the electronics research lab, which did basic and unclassified research, and the applied laboratory, which did classified research and gave up
cues.zh: 为了他们的核武器。这一切不仅需要照片证据，还需要电子情报和信号情报。于是斯坦福也加入进来，踏入了这个“黑色世界”。特曼决定把从事基础性、非机密研究的电子研究实验室，与从事机密研究的应用实验室合并，

cues.en: and merged them both. Stanford in 1955 set up the Systems Engineering Lab and became the most advanced signals intelligence, telemetry intelligence facility for its government customers. Now, in the context of the time, I'm not making any moral or value judgments about whether this is good or bad. But I will tell you the thing that Terman was doing at the same time, which changed all your lives.
cues.zh: 把两者合为一体。斯坦福在1955年设立了系统工程实验室，成为其政府客户最先进的信号情报、遥测情报设施。在当时的历史背景下，我不对这是好是坏做任何道德或价值判断。但我要告诉你特曼同时做的另一件事，这件事改变了你们所有人的生活，

cues.en: which is why you're here. He did something, I don't think he gets any credit for it at all. And he changed the rules in how startups and universities work together. He was the first engineering dean and provost to encourage and almost throw out graduate students to start companies here in Silicon Valley. He encourages professors to consult for those companies. And he encouraged professors to take board seats, advisory board roles,
cues.zh: 也就是你们今天坐在这里的原因。他做了一件了不起的事，我觉得他几乎没有因此得到任何赞誉。他改变了初创公司和大学合作的游戏规则。他是第一位鼓励、甚至可以说是把研究生“推出去”在硅谷创业的工程学院院长兼教务长。他鼓励教授为这些公司做顾问，

cues.en: anything you can to help new nascent startups. And he made it easy to walk out of Stanford with all this technology, like some other companies we might know, with incredibly easy terms. And in fact, at Stanford, getting out into the real world was good for your academic career, rather than bad. Contrast this to any other environment in the mid 1950s. Now, back to the war, the Cold War.
cues.zh: 鼓励教授担任董事、顾问委员会成员，总之尽一切可能去帮助新生的初创公司。他还让带着这些技术走出斯坦福变得非常容易，就像我们知道的其他一些公司一样，条件宽松得不可思议。事实上，在斯坦福，投身现实世界对你的学术生涯是有益的，而不是有害的。对比一下上世纪50年代中期的其他任何地方。好了，回到战争，冷战。

cues.en: Stanford was helping the military understand the electronic order of battle. We believed our bombers were going to have to one day penetrate the Soviet Union. And just like everything we learned about doing that over occupied Europe, we're going to have to relearn again. Where are the radars? The Strategic Air Command needed to know and the CIA needed to know for a reason I'll show you in a second. What were the technical details of those radars?
cues.zh: Stanford 当时在帮助军方理解电子战斗序列。我们相信，我们的轰炸机总有一天要深入苏联。就像我们在被占领的欧洲上空做这件事时学到的一切一样，我们得重新再学一遍。雷达在哪里？战略空军司令部需要知道，CIA 也需要知道，原因我马上会展示给你们。那些雷达的技术细节是什么？

cues.en: The NSA and CIA needed to give that detail to their contractors to build jammers. The periphery, that is the outside of the Soviet Union, its radar order of battle was somewhat known. Because you could fly a plane right to the Soviet border, radars would turn on, fighters would come out, and you would know, yep, there are radars there that are trying to kill us. But you had no idea what was going on inside the middle of the country.
cues.zh: NSA 和 CIA 需要把这些细节交给承包商，用来制造干扰机。外围，也就是苏联的外部，其雷达战斗序列多少是已知的。因为你可以把飞机一直飞到苏联边境，雷达会开机，战斗机会出动，你就会知道：没错，那里有雷达想干掉我们。但你根本不知道这个国家腹地内部发生了什么。

cues.en: This wasn't an academic exercise. Over 23 planes were shot down. In the middle of the Cold War, all of them electronic intelligence gathering planes that flew along the periphery of the Soviet Union trying to record and identify the early warning radars that bombers would first see. Over 200 U.S. citizens were shot down. Some of them interned and never were released.
cues.zh: 这不是学术演练。有超过 23 架飞机被击落。在冷战中期，它们全都是电子情报侦察机，沿着苏联外围飞行，试图记录并识别轰炸机首先会看到的预警雷达。有 200 多名美国公民被击落。其中一些人被扣押，再也没被释放。

cues.en: This is a hot, cold war. Now, some of you might have heard of a plane called the U-2. Anybody hear of that airplane? Now, any time I heard of the U-2, I saw those great photos. And the U-2, that was a photo plane. Turns out, by weight, most of the payload was electronic intelligence gathering equipment. But till today, you'll never read about that, about the U-2 payload being Eland. It was all about cameras.
cues.zh: 这是一场热化的冷战。现在，你们有些人可能听说过一种叫 U-2 的飞机。有人听说过那架飞机吗？每当我听到 U-2，我看到的都是那些精彩照片。而 U-2，那是一架照相侦察机。结果发现，按重量算，大部分有效载荷都是电子情报搜集设备。但直到今天，你都不会读到这些，不会读到 U-2 的有效载荷是 ELINT。大家讲的都是相机。

cues.en: Turns out, yes, we were trying to take pictures, but more so, we were trying to understand across the interior of the Soviet Union what was the electronic order of battle. And the equipment that did that was courtesy of Stanford and Silicon Valley. System that went from 150 megahertz to 40 gigahertz, Stanford Electronics Lab. Jammers to keep surface-to-air missiles away, Granger Associates, Watkins-Johnson's, et cetera.
cues.zh: 事实证明，确实如此，我们当时是在试图拍照，但更重要的是，我们试图了解苏联内陆的电子战斗序列。而完成这项任务的设备来自斯坦福和硅谷。系统频率从150兆赫兹到40吉赫兹，出自斯坦福电子实验室。用于驱离地空导弹的干扰机，来自Granger Associates、Watkins-Johnson等公司。

cues.en: The U-2s were jam-packed with E-Lint receivers. Now, what's interesting was the innovation that came out of this. Just a side story. In 1960, at what was then Cape Canaveral, the Air Force was launching a rocket. And they noticed that radar signals from a radar that had nothing to do with this test somehow was bouncing off this missile when it was in the air and was picked up by another radar.
cues.zh: U-2侦察机上塞满了电子情报接收机。有意思的是由此产生的创新。顺便讲个故事。1960年，在当时的卡纳维拉尔角，空军正在发射一枚火箭。他们注意到，某个与此次试验毫无关系的雷达发出的信号，竟然在导弹飞行时从导弹上反射，并被另一部雷达接收到。

cues.en: Two separate radars, transmitter, receiver, completely separate, happened to be bouncing off an ICBM as it was being tested. They said, huh, this is kind of interesting. And they basically came up with the idea of a bi-static intercept receiver. That is, let's use a separate transmitter and receiver and a non-cooperating thing in the middle. And they said, where on earth could we actually use this?
cues.zh: 两部独立的雷达，发射机和接收机完全分开，恰好在一枚洲际弹道导弹试射时从弹体上反射了信号。他们说，嘿，这挺有意思。于是他们基本上提出了双基地截获接收机的构想。也就是说，用一个独立的发射机和接收机，中间放一个不配合的目标。他们问，我们到底能在哪儿用上这个？

cues.en: to get some more information about radars in the middle of the Soviet Union. So Project Melody was born. And it turns out the Soviets were testing their ICBMs in the southwest corner of Soviet Union. So we used their missiles as they were launched to pick up the radar transmissions of their radars inside the Soviet Union and receive them.
cues.zh: 来获取一些关于苏联内陆雷达的情报。于是“旋律计划”诞生了。结果发现，苏联人正在苏联西南角试射他们的洲际弹道导弹。于是我们就利用他们发射的导弹，去截获苏联境内雷达的发射信号并加以接收。

cues.en: and our receiving stations in Iran. It produced intercepts of all the Soviet ground-based missile tracking radars, including ABM radars and ballistic missile radars. We had no idea existed. Somebody got a medal for this one. The other thing we were building at the time after the U-2 was another intelligence platform called the Oskarter A-12. It was the U-2 successor. The public name for this was the SR-71. Now, this was a CIA plane.
cues.zh: 包括我们在伊朗的接收站。它截获了苏联所有地基导弹跟踪雷达的信号，包括反导雷达和弹道导弹雷达，其中有些我们根本不知道存在。为此有人还拿了奖章。当时我们在 U-2 之后还在造的另一个平台，是一种叫 OXCART 的 A-12 情报飞机。它是 U-2 的后继机型，对外公开的名字就是 SR-71。而这其实是一架中情局的飞机。

cues.en: And the CIA was really concerned about how vulnerable this plane might be at high altitude because it was designed to fly at above 80,000 feet at Mach 3. And it realized from the time it designed it to the time it was thinking about flying it over the Soviet Union that the Soviet air defense system had gotten really dense. So the UN staff office of the CIA said, what's the radar environment like in the Soviet Union? And they needed to find
cues.zh: 中情局非常担心这架飞机在高空会有多脆弱，因为它被设计为在 3 马赫的速度下于 8 万英尺以上高度飞行。而且他们从设计之初到打算让它飞越苏联上空时，就意识到苏联的防空系统已经变得非常密集。于是中情局的参谋办公室问：苏联的雷达环境到底怎么样？他们需要找到

cues.en: information about a radar called Tall King. It was the primary Soviet air defense radar, 100 feet wide, ranged 375 miles. And we were interested on where they were located. B-52 bombers needed to know. This A-12 ox card plane needed to know. The problem with signal intelligence, of course, it's all a line of sight. The radar was inside the Soviet Union, and none of our Eland aircraft could get high enough.
cues.zh: 一种叫 Tall King 的雷达的相关情报。它是苏联主要的防空雷达，宽 100 英尺，探测距离 375 英里。我们想知道它们部署在哪里。B-52 轰炸机需要知道，这架 OXCART A-12 飞机也需要知道。但信号情报的问题在于，全都是视距传播。雷达在苏联境内，我们的电子情报侦察机没有一架能飞得足够高

cues.en: to pick up the signals. So what we decided to do was to use the moon. We're going to use the moon as a bi-static reflector. And we're going to listen for tall king signals as the Earth revolved and rotated around. And the alignment happened like an hour or two a month. But if you had multiple big radar dishes, you actually could start plotting the position of tall king radars. And it turns out this was tested in New Jersey at Bell Labs.
cues.zh: 来接收信号。所以我们决定利用月球。我们要把月球当作一个双基地反射器，在地球公转和自转的过程中监听 Tall King 的信号。这种对齐条件一个月大概只有一两个小时。但如果你有多台大型雷达天线，你其实就能开始标绘出 Tall King 雷达的位置。事实证明，这项试验是在新泽西州的贝尔实验室做的。

cues.en: And they said, late 1950s, holy cow, this really works, but we don't have enough geographic separation. We need more big dishes, big dish. Big dishes all of a sudden get funded in the late 50s. Pay for and develop the Stanford dish. Hide the relationships through cover agencies. All you needed was access to the dish about an hour or two a month.
cues.zh: 他们当时说，那是上世纪50年代末，天哪，这招真管用，但我们的地域覆盖还不够。我们需要更多的大型天线，大型天线。于是大型天线在50年代末突然就拿到了经费。出资建造了斯坦福大天线。用掩护机构把这种关系隐藏起来。其实每月只需要使用天线一两个小时就够了。

cues.en: Oh, we have some researchers coming in. Don't worry. And they didn't. They didn't take up much time. And this only lasted four or five years until we put other systems in place. But all the dishes that happened to get funded, you think we were really interested in radio astronomy in that order of magnitude? And we even built a bigger one at Sugar Grove in Virginia, a steerable dish, and the Jerome Bank dish in the UK all of a sudden got funded as well.
cues.zh: “哦，我们有研究人员要来用。”别担心。实际上他们也没占用多少时间。这种情况只持续了四五年，直到我们建成了其他系统。但那些碰巧拿到经费的天线，你以为我们真有那么大的兴趣搞射电天文学？我们甚至在弗吉尼亚州的舒格格罗夫建了个更大的可转动天线，英国的耶罗姆·班克天线也突然拿到了经费。

cues.en: We finally figured out where the tall kings were, but one of the things we were interested in was now that we know where they are, we need to know more stuff about them for jamming and stealth. So the solution for this was to build a fleet of electronic intelligence planes that literally, once in air, unspooled antennas that were miles long. I'm talking about miles. Flew around the periphery of the Soviet Union, measured the Soviet air defense, and basically said,
cues.zh: 我们终于搞清了那些“高个子国王”的位置，但我们感兴趣的另一件事是，既然知道它们在哪了，我们就需要了解更多信息，用于干扰和隐身。解决方案是组建一支电子情报机队，这些飞机升空后 literally 展开数英里长的天线。我说的是好几英里。它们沿着苏联周边飞行，测量苏联的防空系统，然后基本得出结论：

cues.en: Holy cow, these guys are pretty good. And it changed the Strategic Air Command's integrated operating plan. So B-52s, which had been designed to fly in at high altitudes, now had to go in at 200 feet. Completely changed the nature of one of our strategic triads. And finally, there was something called Project Palladium. It said, OK, we know how good all this other stuff is, but we need to know how sensitive the equipment is and how good are their operators.
cues.zh: “天哪，这帮家伙还挺厉害的。”这改变了战略空军司令部的整体作战计划。原本设计从高空突防的B-52，现在得从200英尺高度进入。这彻底改变了我们战略三元之一的核心性质。最后还有一个叫“钯金计划”的项目。它提出：好吧，我们已经知道这些装备有多厉害了，但我们还需要知道他们的设备灵敏度有多高，操作员水平又有多强。

cues.en: And so what we built was a system here in Silicon Valley, a company to be unnamed, that electronically generated false targets into the Soviet radars. They saw ghost aircraft. And we could simulate any aircraft, any speed. And the trick, though, is to know what were they seeing? So we trained a team with the National Security Agency to listen to the communications channels of the radar operators while we were injecting false signals.
cues.zh: 于是我们在硅谷建了一套系统，公司名字不便透露，它能以电子方式向苏联雷达注入假目标。他们看到的是幽灵飞机。我们能模拟任何飞机、任何速度。但关键在于，得知道他们到底看到了什么。所以我们和国家安全局一起训练了一支团队，在我们注入假信号时监听雷达操作员的通信频道。

cues.en: And so we could decrypt them in real time. Thank you, National Semiconductor, which is another story. And watch when they turned on their tracking radars. And we used ground bases, naval ships, submarines. And this lasted about three years, gathered enormous data on the sensitivity of the Soviet air defense system. Finally, we had satellites. One of the first satellites we put in space was an electronic intelligence satellite, Project Grab.
cues.zh: 这样我们就能实时解密他们的通信。感谢 National Semiconductor，那又是另一个故事了。我们还能观察他们何时开启跟踪雷达。我们动用了地面基地、海军舰艇、潜艇。这持续了大约三年，收集了大量关于苏联防空系统灵敏度的数据。最后，我们有了卫星。我们送入太空的首批卫星之一是一颗电子情报卫星，代号 Project Grab。

cues.en: All of a sudden we no longer needed to use the moon. We can just now use a satellite going around, collect radar emissions from Soviet air defense radars when it got over a ground station, dump out position, latitude, frequency, et cetera, built by the Naval Research Laboratory and used by Strategic Air Command. Then the Navy put some stuff in space, except this time it wasn't one satellite. They put a whole cloud of them up and allowed them to direction find.
cues.zh: 突然间，我们不再需要借助月球了。我们可以直接用一颗绕轨卫星，在飞越地面站时收集苏联防空雷达的辐射信号，然后回传位置、纬度、频率等信息，这由海军研究实验室建造，供战略空军司令部使用。后来海军也往太空部署了一些东西，只不过这次不是一颗卫星。他们一次性部署了一整群，让它们进行测向。

cues.en: on radio and radar signals that Soviet ships were using in the middle of the ocean. Now for the first time, you couldn't hide anywhere in the ocean. Clusters of satellites triangulated and direction-fined. What does this have to do with Silicon Valley? And as an example, just of one of the contractors, many that exist in this valley. Sylvania, who you might think of as being a light bulb manufacturer,
cues.zh: 通过无线电和雷达信号，侦测苏联船只在海洋中央的活动。现在第一次，你在海洋中无处可藏。卫星群进行三角定位和方向测定。这跟硅谷有什么关系？举个例子，就拿这个山谷里众多承包商之一来说。Sylvania，你可能以为它是灯泡制造商，

cues.en: was the second largest employer in Silicon Valley in the late 1950s. They ran the electronics defense laboratory, which is basically an electronic countermeasures lab. Terman was a consultant, half the professors in the electronic labs were consultants. 1,300 employees, big deal. But the bigger deal is in 1964, their director thought it was the world's biggest bureaucracy and quit and founded a company called ESL. Anybody know what happened to Bill Perry?
cues.zh: 在1950年代末是硅谷第二大雇主。他们运营电子防御实验室，基本上是一个电子对抗实验室。Terman是顾问，电子实验室一半教授是顾问。1300名员工，很了不起。但更了不起的是1964年，他们的主管认为这是世界上最大的官僚机构，于是辞职创办了一家叫ESL的公司。有人知道Bill Perry后来怎么样了吗？

cues.en: father of stealth became the secretary of defense. Biggest spook in Silicon Valley, father of stealth, direct descendant of Terman in terms of military industrial relationships. Terman's legacy was the father of the relationship between the university and the military, began an institutionalized black Silicon Valley, ESL, Lockheed, GTL, Sylvania, Argo.
cues.zh: 隐形技术之父成了国防部长。硅谷最大的间谍头子，隐形技术之父，在军工关系上是Terman的直系传人。Terman的遗产是大学与军方关系的奠基者，开启了制度化的黑色硅谷：ESL、Lockheed、GTL、Sylvania、Argo。

cues.en: The university is a hand-in-hand collaborator with startups. It's probably his most lasting legacy. But the black version of what he did is completely missing from any of his histories or biographies. You'll never see anybody talk about what Terman did at all post-World War II. But the good stuff, the stuff that's lasting, the stuff that in fact makes us all here today, is he developed this model.
cues.zh: 大学是初创企业的携手合作者。这可能是他最持久的遗产。但他所做的黑色版本完全缺失于任何历史或传记中。你永远看不到有人谈论Terman在二战后做了什么。但好的东西，持久的东西，事实上让我们今天齐聚于此的东西，是他开发了这个模式。

cues.en: for university and entrepreneurial partnerships, consulting, patents, intellectual property, this notion of equity. All came from Terman. A really unique guy. Now, normally I would end this story right here. But I thought I'd tell you story five for two minutes. Unintended consequences.
cues.zh: 为大学与创业合作、咨询、专利、知识产权，以及股权这个概念。全都源自特曼。一个非常独特的人。通常我会在这里结束这个故事。但我想用两分钟讲讲第五个故事。意外后果。

cues.en: University and industry relationships are the most visible part of his legacy. And the deep and pervasive university intelligence relationships are his secret legacy. But remember, what did Terman think the value was going to turn out to be? Anybody remember what he said it was? It was military, klystrons, microwaves, electronics. We're not the microwave valley, are we? How come? And here's why it's Silicon Valley. On the other side of town,
cues.zh: 大学与产业的关系是他遗产中最显眼的部分。而深厚而广泛的大学情报关系是他的秘密遗产。但记住，特曼认为价值最终会是什么？有人记得他说过是什么吗？是军事、速调管、微波、电子。我们不是微波谷，对吧？为什么？这就是为什么它是硅谷。在镇子的另一边，

cues.en: The head of radar bombing training from the Air Force starts a company. Remember these guys? This is a World War II bombing radar video.
cues.zh: 空军雷达轰炸训练负责人创办了一家公司。还记得这些人吗？这是一段二战轰炸雷达视频。

cues.en: Radar equipment consists of a radio transmitter and receiver. The transmitter sends a radio beam earthward. If it strikes water, the beam is not reflected. The receiver picks up nothing and the scope appears dark, as it is now over the Pacific Ocean. But if the beam strikes a solid object such as land, it's reflected and shows light on the scope. Watch. Something's coming in now at the upper left.
cues.zh: 雷达设备由一个无线电发射器和接收器组成。发射器向地面发送无线电波束。如果碰到水，波束不会被反射。接收器什么都收不到，屏幕上显示为暗，就像现在在太平洋上空一样。但如果波束碰到固体物体比如陆地，就会被反射并在屏幕上显示为亮。看。现在左上角有东西进来了。

cues.en: Adjusting the receiver control sharpens the picture. There they are, two islands both with mountains on them. That should make them easy to identify. It's Hawaii. Turns out that this was really hard to do, that is to pick up these signals and figure out what land masses there were. It was so hard, the Air Force put, or Army Air Force put together a training group to build map overlays.
cues.zh: 调整接收器控制可以锐化图像。它们在那里，两座岛，上面都有山。这应该让它们容易识别。是夏威夷。结果发现这真的很难做到，也就是捕捉这些信号并弄清楚有哪些陆地。太难了，空军，或者说陆军航空队，组建了一个训练小组来制作地图叠加层。

cues.en: And there was one guy who was responsible for all this in World War II. This is the guy who started a company. At the same time, Terman's working on all these black projects. He was also director of the Navy anti-submarine warfare operations at Columbia, head of the radar bombing training for the Air Force. Anybody know who this guy is? He was deputy director of all of weapons systems and valuation. He was helping us build ICBMs. He was the deputy director.
cues.zh: 二战期间，有个人对这一切都负有责任。他就是创办了一家公司的那个人。与此同时，Terman 在做各种机密项目。他还担任哥伦比亚大学海军反潜作战行动主任，以及空军雷达轰炸训练负责人。有人知道他是谁吗？他曾任武器系统与评估部门副主任。他还帮我们研发洲际弹道导弹。他是副主任。

cues.en: Who's this guy? He's a co-inventor of the transistor, and he founded Shockley Semiconductor. He's William Shockley, father of Silicon Valley. William Shockley is the reason why we have all these semiconductor companies in Silicon Valley. He was a great researcher, awesome talent spotter, and the worst manager probably on the planet. Unintended consequences, he hires the world's best team, and eight of them leave two years later, including Robert Noyce.
cues.zh: 这人是谁？他是晶体管的共同发明者，还创办了 Shockley Semiconductor。他就是 William Shockley，硅谷之父。正是 William Shockley，才有了硅谷这么多半导体公司。他是出色的研究者，也是慧眼识人的伯乐，但管理能力恐怕是全世界最差的。结果适得其反：他招来一支顶尖团队，两年后其中八个人离开，包括 Robert Noyce。

cues.en: and Gordon Moore. And this group of eight found Fairchild Semiconductor, which then becomes the father of almost every other chip company in Silicon Valley. By the way, his beliefs about eugenics just effectively end any type of commercial career in 1963. But what he did for semiconductors, basically, he's at the root. All flowed from him. And Silicon Valley
cues.zh: 还有 Gordon Moore。这八个人创办了 Fairchild Semiconductor，后来它成了硅谷几乎所有其他芯片公司的源头。顺带一提，他对优生学的看法，实际上让他在 1963 年彻底断送了商业生涯。但他对半导体产业的贡献，基本上就是一切的根源。一切都由此而来。硅谷

cues.en: It became Silicon Valley because of the guy who did radar bombing training in World War II. The legacy military R&D put millions of dollars into the valley. Excuse me, billions of dollars. Secrecy limited, as it does, the diffusion of direct technology breakthroughs. But the biggest benefit is the one we never would have figured out. It was the university industry collaborations since most lasting benefit. So that's it. Thank you for your time. And hope it was interesting.
cues.zh: 之所以成为硅谷，是因为那位在二战期间负责雷达轰炸训练的人。军事研发留下的遗产，为硅谷投入了数百万美元。不，是数十亿美元。保密固然限制了直接技术突破的传播，但最大的好处却是我们从未预料到的：大学与产业界的合作，这才是最持久的成果。就这样。谢谢大家抽出时间。希望大家觉得这场演讲有意思。

cues.en: I'll take any questions if there are any. Yes. So it turns out, thank you. So the question was, how come during the Battle of Britain the Germans weren't smart enough to shut down the British air defense system called chain home radar? And it turns out that's one of the ironies of the war, that the chain home radar sites were so primitive they operated at a frequency below.
cues.zh: 大家有问题都可以提。好，那位。其实是这样，谢谢。问题是：为什么在不列颠空战期间，德国人没聪明到去摧毁被称为 Chain Home 雷达的英国防空系统？事实证明，这是二战的一大讽刺，Chain Home 雷达站太原始了，其工作频率甚至低于……

cues.en: what the German electronic intelligence systems actually could detect. No joke, because the Germans, and in post war we all asked her, here these guys understood all this stuff. Turned out chain home was a variable frequency radar system. It barely worked, but it barely meant it worked. So the British were able to scramble fighters rather than having them orbit all the time, in time to intercept the
cues.zh: 德国电子情报系统实际能够探测到的范围。真没开玩笑，战后我们发现，德国人自以为对这些了如指掌。结果 Chain Home 是个变频雷达系统。它勉强能工作，但“勉强”也意味着确实管用。所以英国人能够及时紧急起飞战斗机，而不必整天在空中盘旋巡逻，从而及时拦截……

cues.en: German bombers during the Blitz. And the Germans never understood the purpose of those tall towers. In fact, there's a long story that the German electronic intelligence system used a Zeppelin pre-World War II breakout to orbit Britain and the radio receiver they had didn't go down that low. Question?
cues.zh: 闪电战期间的德国轰炸机。德国人始终没搞懂那些高塔是干什么用的。实际上，二战爆发前还有个传闻：德国电子情报部门曾用齐柏林飞艇绕英国飞行侦察，但他们带的无线电接收机探测频段根本没那么低。还有问题吗？

cues.en: air defense system. How did we do that without actual planes? So the question was, how did we inject false signals into the Soviet Eastern Bloc radar systems? How did we do that without planes? And so that falls under the, if I told you I'd have to kill you. But the technique is.
cues.zh: 防空系统。在没有真机的情况下，我们是怎么做到的？问题是：我们当时是如何向苏联东欧集团的雷达系统注入虚假信号的？没有飞机我们又是怎么做到的？这就属于“我要是告诉你，就得把你灭口”那类机密了。不过这项技术其实是……

cues.en: It may or may not be an open literature. You can inject signals. The spoofing stuff was used extensively, even in the first, in the two Gulf wars, used in Vietnam, et cetera. Other questions? Yes. One of your things was a list of the pilots who were shot down by the Soviet defenses. Why are all the names of the pilots actually found with their Americans? So the question is, the list of the pilots who were shot down.
cues.zh: 它可能属于公开文献，也可能不是。你可以注入信号。欺骗手段被广泛使用，最早在海湾战争中就用过，也在越南战争中用过，等等。还有问题吗？有。你提到过一份名单，上面列着被苏联防空力量击落的飞行员。为什么名单上的飞行员名字，都是和美国人一起被找到的？所以问题是，那份被击落飞行员的名单。

cues.en: How come the names were Russian sounding? The pilots on that list were the names of the Russian pilots who shot down the planes. When I said this was open source, that list came from the ex-Soviet Union. Just to continue that conversation, one of the things we also did, which almost started World War III, is not only did we probe the periphery, pre-U2 we flew electronic intelligence planes all the way across.
cues.zh: 怎么名字听起来都像俄罗斯人？名单上列的是击落飞机的俄罗斯飞行员。我说这是开源资料时，指的就是那份来自前苏联的名单。接着刚才的话题，我们还做过一件差点引发第三次世界大战的事：我们不只侦察外围，在U-2之前，还驾驶电子情报飞机一路飞越。

cues.en: the length and breadth of the Soviet Union, just to gather electronic intelligence. That's how blind the strategic air command was and how desperate they were to gather this data. Other questions? Yes. So how much of this stuff fell into Soviet's hands? The Soviet Union had a active, very active,
cues.zh: 苏联的各个地区，只为收集电子情报。战略空军司令部当时就是这么缺乏情报，也这么迫切地想收集这些数据。还有问题吗？有。苏联人掌握了多少这类情报？苏联在美国设有一个活跃、非常活跃的

cues.en: espionage ring in the United States and particularly targeted one main branch of it at Silicon Valley. And while we all think of the KGB, and that's whose records we actually got access to, one of the more effective groups for espionage was the GRU, which was the Soviet military's intelligence. Targeted almost every defense contractor in Silicon Valley, and that role has now been passed on to the Chinese. Other questions? In the back.
cues.zh: 间谍网，尤其把其中一支主力部署在硅谷。我们都知道克格勃，而我们实际拿到的也是克格勃的档案。不过，最有效的间谍组织之一是GRU，也就是苏联军方的情报机构。它几乎盯上了硅谷所有的国防承包商，如今这项任务已经转交给中国人了。还有问题吗？后排。

cues.en: You talked about gathering colleges over the Soviet Union. Where was the war being done for protecting the U.S. against the Soviet colleges?
cues.zh: 你谈到了在苏联各地汇集院校。为保护美国免受苏联院校威胁，这场战争是在哪里进行的？

cues.en: One of the things we built in the US was something called SAGE. And for those of you who haven't been to the Computer History Museum, it was stood for Semi Automated Ground Environment. But it was the first automated air defense system, which really was a spectacular piece of hardware and software in the late 50s. It ran operationally for about 20 plus years. Probably one of the most sophisticated pieces of integrated man-machine user interface came out with the first light guns.
cues.zh: 我们在美国建造的东西之一叫 SAGE。没去过 Computer History Museum 的人可能不知道，它代表 Semi Automated Ground Environment。但它是第一套自动化防空系统，在 50 年代末确实是软硬件上的杰作。它实际运行了 20 多年。大概最复杂的集成人机用户界面之一，还配上了最早的光枪。

cues.en: It's just worth walking next door and taking a look at it in Mountain View. And there were other centers of excellence in the U.S. Around Route 128. For those of you who haven't read Annalee Saxinian's book called Regional Advantage, until the 70s it wasn't clear that Silicon Valley or Route 128 was going to be the winner in the center of U.S. innovation.
cues.zh: 值得去隔壁，在 Mountain View 看一眼。美国还有其他卓越中心，在 Route 128 附近。没读过 Annalee Saxinian 那本《Regional Advantage》的人可能不知道，直到 70 年代，还不清楚 Silicon Valley 和 Route 128 谁会成为美国创新中心的赢家。

cues.en: posits some very interesting hypotheses about why it happened here rather than there. But around 128 and around Washington DC, there were a lot of innovative electronics, military industrial electronics companies. Other questions? OK. Thank you very much, and thanks for your time.
cues.zh: 它提出了一些非常有趣的假设，解释为什么发生在这里而不是那里。但在 Route 128 和 Washington DC 附近，有很多创新型电子公司、军工电子公司。还有其他问题吗？好。非常感谢，也谢谢大家的时间。
